ety.text: From Middle English joinen, joynen, joignen, from Old French joindre, juindre, jungre, from Latin iungō (“join, yoke”, verb), from Proto-Indo-European *yewg- (“to join, unite”). Cognate with Old English iucian, iugian, ġeocian, ġyċċan (“to join; yoke”). More at yoke.

senses.d: To connect or combine into one; to put together.
ex: The plumber joined the two ends of the broken pipe.
We joined our efforts to get an even better result.

senses.d: To come together; to meet.
ex: Parallel lines never join.
These two rivers join in about 80 miles.

senses.d: To enter into association or alliance, to unite in a common purpose.
ex:
Forſake thy king and do but ioyne with me
And we will triumph ouer al the world.
[…]Nature and Fortune ioyn’d to make thee great.

senses.d: To start working on or participating in a project.
ex: He joined season 2 of the television show.

senses.d: To come into the company of.
ex: I will join you in watching the football game as soon as I have finished my work.

senses.d: To become a member of.
ex: Many children join a sports club.
Most politicians have joined a party.

senses.d: To produce an intersection of data in two or more database tables.
ex: By joining the Customer table on the Product table, we can show each customer's name alongside the products they have ordered.

senses.d: To unite in marriage.
ex: Into the whiche holy eſtate theſe two perſones pꝛeſent: come nowe to be ioyned.

[…]this fellow wil but ioyne you together, as they ioyne
 Wainscot, then one of you wil proue a ſhrunke pannell[…]

senses.d: To enjoin upon; to command.
ex: And they ioyne them penaunce / as they call it / to faſt / to goo pylgremages ⁊ geve ſo moch to make ſatiſfaccion with all.

senses.d: To accept, or engage in, as a contest.
ex: to join encounter, battle, or issue

Then when our powers in points of ſwords are ioin’d
And cloſde in compaſſe of the killing bullet, […]

senses.d: The lowest upper bound, an operation between pairs of elements in a lattice, denoted by the symbol ∨.
The smallest linear space containing both of two given linear spaces.

The noun is from Middle English joynt (attested since the late 13th century), from Old French joint (“joint of the body”) (attested since the 12th century). The adjective (attested since the 15th century) is from Old French jointiz. Both Old French words are from Latin iūnctus, the past participle of iungō. See also join, jugular, junction. Displaced Old English fōg and partially displaced English lith.

senses.d: United, combined
ex: the joint influences of culture and climate

senses.d: Done by two or more people or organisations working together.
ex: The play was a joint production between the two companies.
A joint burden laid upon us all.

senses.d: The point where two components of a structure join, but are still able to rotate.
ex: This rod is free to swing at the joint with the platform.

senses.d: The point where two components of a structure join rigidly.
ex: The water is leaking out of the joint between the two pipes.

senses.d: Any part of an animalian body where two bones or exoskeleton segments are abutted, in most cases allowing that part of the body to be bent or straightened.
The means of securing together the meeting surfaces of components of a structure.
ex: The dovetail joint, while more difficult to make, is also quite strong.

senses.d: A cut of meat, especially (but not necessarily) (a) one containing a joint in the sense of an articulation or (b) one rolled up and tied.
ex: Near-synonym: roast
Set the joint in a roasting tin and roast for the calculated cooking time.

senses.d: The part or space included between two joints, knots, nodes, or articulations.
ex: a joint of cane or of a grass stem; a joint of the leg

senses.d: A fracture in which the strata are not offset; a geologic joint.

A place of business, particularly in the food service or hospitality industries; sometimes extended to any place that is a focus of human connection or activity (e.g., schools, hangouts, party spots).
ex: It was the kind of joint you wouldn't want your boss to see you in.
"...Where's the ladies' in this joint? I've to powder me nose."

senses.d: A place of resort for tramps.

ex: to joint boards
a jointing plane

senses.d: To join; to connect; to unite; to combine.
ex:
But soon that war had end, and the time's state
Made friends of them, jointing their force 'gainst Caesar

senses.d: To provide with a joint or joints; to articulate.
ex: The fingers are […]jointed together for motion.

senses.d: To separate the joints; of; to divide at the joint or joints; to disjoint; to cut up into joints, as meat.
ex: He joints the neck.

senses.d: To fit as if by joints; to coalesce as joints do.
ex: the stones joint, neatly.
